Preface
Welcome to the beta version of the upcoming Open Urban Morphology Guidebook. This book is intended for students in urbanism, architecture and other building sciences who want to know more about morphological urban analysis techniques and their application.
The guidebook is intended as a practical tool. It gives some basic information on methodology and history, but the emphasis is mostly on showing examples students may find inspirational or helpful in their design research.
The book is interactive in that there are many crosslinks throughout, making it easy to jump from example to example. It is open to the extent that copyright restrictions prevent us from using most of the original drawings.
In the coming years, we want to add to the present core many more drawings produced by our teachers, students and other users. For now, we are interested in a proof of concept, and we invite you to let us know what you think.
We hope that – in due course – the Open Urban Morphology Guidebook will prove to be a useable resource for design students and researchers alike.
If you want to get in touch to share your experience, please send an email to the editors: c.forgaci@tudelft.nl or l.p.j.vandenburg@tudelft.nl.
The Open Urban Morphology Guidebook was made possible by financial support from the TU-Delft Open Education Stimulation Fund.

title: 2  Foundations and Frontiers
text:
Introduction
Cities are physical archives of conscious spatial decisions and countless unintended events. When we walk the street, when we navigate with a map in our hands, or when we read about a place as visitors, we can see glimpses of this rich history. As professionals, we need to do research on urban form in a more systematic way, but essentially, we use the same techniques: we read maps, we document how a city is experienced at eye level, and we look for additional supporting data. In this way, we try to uncover hidden spatial patterns in a city. This study we call Urban Morphology and it remains an essential item in the urbanist’s toolbox.
In this open guidebook on Urban Morphology, we set out to trace the foundations and frontiers of the field and, building on that, to provide urbanism students with a state-of-the-art overview on how to employ urban morphology analytical methods. We hope this will allow for a better understanding of the rules governing urban development but also help to make better design decisions.

title: 2  Foundations and Frontiers
text:
Foundations
Morphology literally means the science of form. The term has its roots in early nineteenth century botany and atonomy. Researchers had already proposed taxonomies of species based on the physical characteristics of plants and animals, but others found this approach to be missing an essential point: there may be countless species, but they appear to share important formal or growth charateristics.  To uncover these, one should study many examples of plants or animals, but an equally important step is to build a mental image of what they all have in common to understand the shared principle of growth. This mental abstraction was called ‘type’. A type does not exist in reality but can be utilised as a proxy to better understand real events. This new science of natural development was coined ‘Morphology’.
In post-WWII urbanism, morphology and the concept of type became key terms1. As in nature, the assumption was that historically, urban development is governed by general and comparable principles of growth and structure. To uncover these, urbanists need to do empirical research into the physical form and development of cities and conceptualise these into types. This will allow designers to make better decisions regarding future development in at least two ways: historical lines of development can be extended in a design proposal, limiting the risk of rupture and thus failure. Second, applying the structural rules embedded within a type in a new design prevents designers from drifting too far off from proven and locally successful spatial solutions.
The promotion of historical continuity, structural integrity and a contextualised approach was seen as extremely important by a new generation of planners, designers and geographers in the nineteen fifties and sixties in a critique of modern planning and design practice. This latter approach, based on a small set of universal spatial principles and backed by scientific projections of, for instance, demographics and economics, had led to many problematic urban extensions and the violation of existing cities. Urban Morphology pioneers countered this development by carefully documenting the spatial qualities of historical cities. By abstracting these in analytical maps and drawings, this knowledge also became available for designers and planners in an attempt to safeguard spatial and historical continuity.
The history of urban morphology and its different schools has been documented extensively, and we don’t have to repeat this here. Although Urban Morphology originated as a critique of modern planning practice, many of its concepts and techniques are still being used today, regardless of their original critical intent. In this Open Urban Analysis Guidebook Morphology, we propose to focus here on three research techniques running through much of the urban morphology literature: map-based analysis, perception-based analysis and data-based analysis. These strands can be read as kinds of analysis that share some common characteristics and position towards urban space and form.

Map-based analysis
We choose map-based analysis as one of our basic categories because for many students and practitioners in urbanism, maps and aerial photographs are the most readily available sources of information. For urbanism professionals, maps are also conventional as a mode of communication and often acquire legal status. Map-based methods are characterised by a strong choice of what is and is not shown, and how (color, contrast, annotations, hierarchies, etc.). This means that maps are inherently political in nature. They are visually powerful and can reveal actual development patterns, but they may also lie or misrepresent. Designers should be aware of this and be careful not to misuse their talents in producing drawings. So, producing maps requires both cartographic knowledge and skills [ref. to key cartography resources] as well as an ethical stance to space production that is often overlooked.
Key examples:

Map-based analysis is a deeply rooted approach going back to Nolli’s figure-ground analysis of Rome;
The Dutch tradition originating in the late seventies, early eighties. Designers like Rein Geurtsen and Maurits de Hoog;
Recent examples include Frits Palmboom’s book ‘Drawing the Ground’ or ‘Barcelona: the Urban Evolution of a Compact City’ by Joan Busquets.



Perception-based analysis
This type of analysis characterises urban space through the eyes of a person (or, why not, a non-human agent) who navigates or uses it. It typically uses eye-level perspectives to systematically (e.g., sequentially) analyse the perception of urban space. Those perspectives can be photographs which are qualitatively analysed, as well as abstractions of reality such as a hand sketch (qualitative) or segmented street view image (quantitative). The perception information can also be further abstracted into mind maps following a method like Lynch’s, for instance. Such abstract map-based notation of course has elements of a map-based analysis, but it remains fundamentally perceptual and subject to interpretation (i.e., two people can draw considerably different maps of the same space). This method will benefit from a good understanding of environmental behaviour and cognition.
Key examples:

Kevin Lynch, Gordon Cullen
Serial vision, scenic approach, human cognition, environmental psychology,
The degree to which a city can be ‘read’ by its users. Open, closed, light, dark, contrasts, how ‘scenes’ are linked through sight lines and other visual clues. Mapping the status quo and then deciding how to improve these.



Data-based analysis
Data-based analyses leverage data, either by combining a large variety of datasets (e.g., in an integrated local analysis) or by extracting patterns from large amounts of data. The main difference from the other two types of analysis is that they answer questions which could not be answered, or at least not fully answered, without data. Typical methods in this category include Space Syntax analysis, quantitative typology analysis, and various other spatial applications of machine learning (e.g., classification of building types based on footprints, prediction of new urban growth locations). These methods also require data analytical skills, including GIS and spatial statistics. We have included data based analysis as a basic category in this book because the desire to quantify urban phenomena has been part of urban research from the early twentieth century onward and continues to attract students. Urban data forever carries with it the promise of a solid, undisputable basis for design. But as with maps, data can be misunderstood or even misused. Data literacy therefore is not complete without a proper awareness of the limits of knowledge to be extracted from data and how to use this knowledge responsibly.

title: 2  Foundations and Frontiers
text:
Frontiers
The three strands of urban morphology have seen considerable methodological and theoretical developments influenced by (1) the increasing availability and diversification of spatial and non-spatial data, computational capacity and related methods and tools, (2) growing attention to sustainability and a maturing body of knowledge on the relationship between spatial/physical form and urban phenomena. Contemporary map-based, perception-based, and data-based urban morphology analyses are increasingly global, evidence-based, collective, and detailed. Methods that were previously limited to a few cases (in the tens) can now be conducted at scale across hundreds or thousands of cases. This has deep implications for the kinds of questions one can ask and the depth of insights one can derive.

New data, methods and tools
An important enabling factor of urban morphology is the increasing availability of open data products. The emergence of Volunteered Geographic Information, most notably through OpenStreetMap (2025), has made urban form data globally available. OpenStreetMap features such as streets, buildings, and points of interest are available with increasing global coverage. Where such data is not available, datasets are generated using machine learning techniques applied to satellite imagery, as in Google’s Open Buildings project (Sirko et al. 2021). Moreover, LiDAR (point-cloud) data provides high-resolution 3D information on building, street and landscape levels—the Dutch digital elevation model AHN4 (2020-2022) is derived from such data. Street-view imagery is also increasingly released as open data products. For instance, the availability of Mapillary data has enabled the creation of the Global Streetscapes dataset (Biljecki et al., 2025). Also, derived products such as segmented street view imagery (i.e., images in which objects and other visible elements or characteristics of a scene have been classified with computer vision) are increasingly made available openly. Moreover, when data is not openly available, methods exist to generate proxies computationally, with a notable example of Voronoi-based partitioning used as a proxy for parcel data (Fleischmann et al., 2020).
[Add a composite image with the types of data mentioned in the paragraph above]
The emergence and increasing availability of data have also led to the development of new tools for processing and analysing those data. Advanced analytical tools are increasingly open and accessible to anyone. Open-source software such as the urban morphology toolkit momepy (Fleischmann, 2019) has enabled automated and scalable workflows. OSMnx (Boeing, 2025) and sfnetworks (van der Meer et al., 2024) allow for programmatic acquisition, processing and analysis of spatial network data. Tools like the street geometry processing toolkit neatnet (Gaboardi et al., 2026) enable the simplification of complex data prior to analysis. While all these tools have made programmatic urban morphology accessible to a growing user base, graphical user interfaces remain the community’s primary choice. Accordingly, the QGIS platform (Graser et al., 2025) and its rapidly evolving ecosystem of plugins have revolutionised spatial analysis and, as part of that, enabled much of contemporary urban morphology analysis. Many of the programmatic tools mentioned above are becoming available as plugins in QGIS’s point-and-click interface.
Such data products, computational methods and tools enable novel research questions, which can lead to both a better understanding of the current situation and potential transformations of an urban space without having to visit it.


Evolving domains of knowledge and application
As shown in Figure #, urban morphology literature shows two major clusters, or domains of knowledge and application, one mostly centred on and extending traditional urban morphology (in red), and one focused on environmental aspects (in green and blue). We elaborate on those two domains in the following two sections.



VOSviewer visualization of keyword co-occurrence from a dataset exported from Scopus on 30 October 2025 using the query “urban morpho*”.



Urban morphometrics
The red cluster represents the longstanding efforts of the field to characterise patterns of urban form, mostly centred on traditional typo-morphology, which is more architectural, fundamental, form-based, and applied to fields of mobility/movement, social behaviour, and spatial perception. With a fundamental focus on form, it is also more design-based than the other cluster. Extending that core, the already half-century-old Space Syntax and quantitative typology-based approaches stand out as the most recent additions. We can refer to this as a quantification of the field of urban morphology, increasingly known as urban morphometrics. While rooted in the form-based cluster, it could also provide a solid basis for the environmental cluster, enhancing large-scale cross-case analysis. Compared with environmental urban morphology approaches, urban morphometrics lacks the third vertical dimension and thus is mostly limited to a two-dimensional understanding of traditional elements of urban form, namely streets, plots, blocks, and buildings.


Environmental urban morphology
The second, larger cluster has emerged recently, continues to grow at an increasing pace and is mostly driven by environmental challenges, such as the urban heat island effect, wind corridors, etc., caused by certain spatial configurations. Materiality and non-built elements also play an important role in the more engineering-focused approach dominating this cluster. This is mostly driven by sustainability challenges, which have been increasingly prominent in urban development agendas. This is known in the literature as environmental urban morphology (Maretto et al., 2023).
The environmental domain is focused on local, computationally intensive approaches. These often use detailed 3D models of the environment that try to capture the complex interplay among factors such as wind, precipitation, and temperature. Assessment of current urban compositions and configurations, and their potential for transformation towards a specific target, plays an important role in this cluster. Spatial Multi-Criteria Decision Analysis (S-MCDA, ref.), spatial typologies augmented with non-spatial environmental performance information, or more advanced machine learning models meant to classify spatial elements or to predict specific environmental performances are commonly employed in this field.



Quality and data literacy
While these recent developments make the field more quantitative, qualitative input (deciding on what to analyse and why) and interpretation (what do the results mean) remain essential. For instance, clustering-based approaches, increasingly used to construct quantitative typologies, require both well-informed input (a meaningful number of clusters) and critical interpretation (what do the clusters mean?). Also, with the increasing availability of real and proxy data, the issue is no longer a lack of information but potentially too much of it. Not least, a theoretical understanding of urban form and its interactions with both social and environmental phenomena remains crucial in quantitative approaches. These issues can only be overcome qualitatively and require critical data literacy.
The analytical skills of an urbanist need to incorporate these recent developments. To what extent, though? What foundational knowledge is necessary for a student of urban morphology to navigate data-augmented contemporary practice of urbanism with competence and confidence? Can we expect urban designers to be experts in machine learning, for instance? What should students learn in the university, and what can they safely encounter only in practice? How do students and teachers position themselves in relation to recent data-producing and data-analytical technologies?

title: 2  Foundations and Frontiers
text:
Morphological analysis and design
For some students, performing urban analysis is perceived as a waste of time because it is unclear how the results of an analysis can be used to improve or even generate design ideas. Conversely, some students will protract the analysis phase unnecessarily as research appears to be less arbitrary than design.
One of the purposes of this book is to provide students in architecture and urbanism with a stronger basis to develop their design ideas on. In this paragraph, we will try to explain how analysis can be used as a powerful design tool.
For the purpose of this book, we say that morphological analysis is a necessary step in the design process. Above, we stated that morphological analysis helps design in at least two ways. It reveals historical growth patterns which an uninformed design may easily break. Also, it unveils typological rules which can safeguard structural integrity in a new design. Seen from this perspective, morphological and typological analysis both support spatial continuity. They have a tendency to sustain the existing, which follows from the critical attitude of its main protagonists. But even if a designer would choose to break with history or existing formal structures, this still necessitates knowledge of these structures. The uninformed alternative – we would argue – is folly and means that a designer has no way of predicting the effects a design proposal might have on its spatial context.
How can morphological analysis be effectively applied in urban design?
This is very straightforward. Morphological analysis reveals spatial patterns or typological rules. We can check the spatial patterns for consistency and use a new design to strengthen or complement these. Similarly, if we distill typological rules from a given location, we can apply these in a new design.
To do this effectively, it is important to use a strong legend. In his famous book ‘The Image of the City’ from 1960, Kevin Lynch introduced five points which he argued are necessary for the design of urban spaces: paths, edges, districts, nodes and landmarks. In drawing maps of Boston with this legend, he was able to see where these needed strengthening. In one of the drawings “Problems of the Boston Image”, Lynch pointed at locations with for instance “direction ambiguity” or “characterless path”, which derive from the original legend. Even though there are no designs included in the book, it is clear now what a designer might do to improve the situation. In the appropriate locations, it must become less ambiguous for people to orient themselves, or a path must acquire a more distinctive spatial character. From this example, we learn that an effective step from analysis to design requires the same legend for both. If we analyse paths and edges, it is because we believe that these are important parameters for design. So think carefully about the items in your legend before you start an analysis, for these are the items you will be working with in your design.

Another example is Gordon Cullen’s famous illustration of what he called ‘serial vision’. Reading his book ‘Townscape’ from 1961, it becomes clear that highlighting sequences of exposure and enclosure, of constraint and relief, and contrasts in scale, style and texture function as ‘legend’ to Cullen’s drawings. Each drawing shows a clear spatial scene, but also reveals what lies ahead in an emerging view. A person moving through a city will constantly look for these visual clues on how to move forward. In the example in the book, these contrasts are particularly strong and clear. Again, if analytical drawings like these reveal that an existing view does not reveal the next step, a designer may work to enhance this through a manipulation of the spatial sequence using contrasts in scale and texture to strengthen exposure.

In data based analyses, Christopher Alexander’s patterns were originally part of a design method where parameters were linked to spatial patterns, which would then be combined into a larger, more complex design. This linear approach has been abandoned. In this book we propose to use data-driven analysis techniques mostly as a tool to evaluate multiple design proposals in a quantitative way. A plan analysis. Data-based analyses can be used not only to describe the current situation but also to make predictions or assess a possible transformation relative to it. How would a new bridge hereimprove safety in this neighbourhood? Which routes could benefit most from this transformed street profile? These are examples of questions that can be answered with a data-based method. As a quantitative approach, this entails making assumptions explicit and working with probabilities. Also, most methods are rather evaluative than generative, meaning that design solutions are not created through data but are rather informed by data-based analysis; the designer is still in the driver’s seat.

title: 7  The Concise Townscape
text:
Why use this method?
These drawings make the reader aware of the many different “scenes” in a city. These scenes can be drawn, named and understood. This is valuable information for urban designers since it represents some of the basic elements in the city and how these are connected through the movement of people. For Cullen, the city has qualities related to space and movement that cannot be represented in 2d. This is not unlike the idea behind the perspective drawings in for example “Elements d’Analyse Urbaine” or “Die Städtebau nach seinen Künstlerischen Grundsätzen”. Cullen proposed no method for design; he primarily wanted to point out the beauty and importance of these spaces in the city. Please note that photographs would not have had the same effect. By drawing, Cullen had to be precise as to what was relevant and what not. His drawings are in fact analyses.

title: 8  Les Bastides: d’Aquitaine, du Bas-Languedoc et du Béarn
text:
Why use this method?
Like in earlier examples of the French and Italian schools of urban analysis, this book on the French Bastides - towns draws heavily on typological research. To isolate the typical, a very large number of towns has been studied on different scale levels. The analysis focuses on the typology of the towns themselves, the relationship of the internal elements such as squares, streets and churches, typology of the building blocks, the typology of the houses and their relation to other elements. Fig. 7.1 shows an idealized layout and how a real Bastide is related to that. As with the Italian analysis of Bologna, the essence of the city is represented in this careful description of the typical. The study implies that an intimate knowledge of this is necessary for architects and urbanists to base their designs on, requiring lengthy and extremely thorough research.

title: 10  The Image of the City
text:
Figure 10.1: Diagram of district. From The Image of the City, by K. Lynch, 1960. Copyright 1960 by the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and the President and Fellows of Harvard College.



A basic point of urban analysis is that the topographical map is not the only one you can draw to represent a city. Kevin Lynch became famous by drawing maps that were reflective of people’s image of a city; their mental maps. Lynch developed drawing techniques to visualise relationships, borders, important places etc. that are perceivable to city dwellers, but are often invisible; at least on a map. Fig. 8.1 shows one of the basic urban configurations that Lynch drew for his book which people use in their image of the city. In Lynch’s view, it is important to be aware of these mental considerations. Knowing how people find their way in a city and what gives cities or areas their specific character can be a valuable tool for design.

title: 12  Typology Construction (quantitative)
text:
Why use this method?
Quantitative typology construction is a core task in urban morphometrics1, as it is meant to reveal patterns in large amounts of data and/or variables that would otherwise be invisible. Compared to qualitative typology construction, it enables the characterisation of large-scale and cross-case patterns.
The underlying quantitative method is cluster analysis, an unsupervised machine learning method which is used to identify a given number of clusters in a dataset. Those clusters are then used to define types that can either simply describe the sought patterns or guide type-specific spatial decisions.

title: 12  Typology Construction (quantitative)
text:
WarningAvoid this frequent mistake!



Typology construction results in a typology that consists of types, not typologies! For example, if you are analysing patterns of variation across urban blocks, the result of your analysis is an urban block typology which consists of, for instance, a closed block type, a green block type and a fragmented block type.

title: 12  Typology Construction (quantitative)
text:
Steps

Define the spatial unit (e.g., building, block, parcel, street, neighbourhood).
Collect relevant morphological variables: direct measurements (e.g., area) or derived metrics (e.g., floor space index). See Fleischmann et al. (2021) for a comprehensive framework of measurable urban form elements.
Use those variables as input in a clustering algorithm (the simplest is k-means). The number of clusters is either defined deductively (you know beforehand how many there should be) or empirically (you try out different numbers of clusters and search for an optimum either quantitatively or qualitatively).
You examine representative cases, which are closest to the cluster centers, to better understand the clusters. Then you name and describe them.

title: 13  Spacematrix
text:
Why use this method?
Understanding urban density is essential for making informed decisions about how cities perform and grow. However, urban density is a rather abstract measure which cannot be easily interpreted. Spacematrix (Pont and Haupt 2023) as a method for urban planning and design tackles this challenge as it allows one to explore the potential of urban density. It combines multiple density indicators, namely Floor Space Index (FSI), Ground Space Index (GSI), Open Space Ratio (OSR) and building height as number of levels (L) into a compound classification of urban form types.

title: 15  3D Scanning and Lidar
text:
Why use this method?
3D scanning, particularly LiDAR (Light Detection and Ranging), is a useful tool for urban analysis, providing precise, high-resolution 3D data of environments. 3D models provide a strong base for a variety of analyses, such as visibility analysis, wind analysis, solar potential, and many others.
3D data of the Netherlands is already available from 3D-BAG, which is an open dataset created in 2008 with 99% validity.
However, especially in your own graduation project, you might find yourself working in sites where such data is incomplete, not so precise, or non-existent altogether. In that case, it can be useful to create your own model using the steps below.

title: 15  3D Scanning and Lidar
text:
How does LiDAR work?
LiDAR is a remote sensing technology that works by emitting laser pulses towards a surface. These pulses travel to the target and back to the sensor and, based on the time it takes for them to return, the system calculates the distance to the target, known as the “time of flight.” Using this distance, the system calculates the exact 3D coordinates (X, Y, Z) of the point where the pulse has reflected, creating a “point” in 3D space. This process is repeated rapidly, generating millions of data points, which together form a dense “point cloud” that can be used to construct highly detailed models of the environment.

LiDAR can be deployed from various platforms: airborne for large-scale mapping, drones for smaller, more specific areas, ground-based for detailed mapping of buildings and infrastructure, and mobile (vehicle-mounted) for road and urban mapping.

In the Favelas 4D project by MIT Senseable City Lab, LiDAR scans taken at street level were used to map Rocinha, the largest favela in Rio de Janeiro. The high precision of the resulting 3D dataset enables morphological analysis of the streets and buildings that constitute this settlement. Informal forms of urbanism are often unrepresented by traditional mapping methods, but here the spatial logics of the favela are made visible.







Figure 15.1: 3D scan of Rocinha favela. From Favelas 4D, by MIT Senseable City Lab, 2021, https://senseable.mit.edu/favelas/. Reproduced with permission.

title: 15  3D Scanning and Lidar
text:
Steps

Obtain data for your point cloud.
Point cloud data can be downloaded from PDOK or AHN for the Netherlands. For other areas, you can check municipal data portals. You can usually download it in the follow formats: LAS, LAZ, PLY, XYZ, or E57. If there is no point cloud data available, go to step 2.
Create your own point cloud. If data for your site already exists, go to step 3.
Depending on your resources and project requirements, you can use different techniques to create a point cloud.

Photogrammetry (using a regular camera or smartphone)
Using a regular camera or smartphone, take several overlapping photos of your chosen object or area from different angles (the bigger the area, the more photographs you will need). You can then use COLMAP to process these images into a point cloud.
iPhone with LiDAR sensor
Newer iPhones (iPhone 12 Pro or later) feature built-in LiDAR sensors, offering better accuracy than regular photos. This allows for detailed, real-time 3D scans. Apps like 3D Scanner App let you create 3D models directly on your phone, making it ideal for small-scale projects.
Drone or airplane (for large-scale projects):
Drones or airplanes equipped with cameras or LiDAR sensors are better for capturing large areas, such as mapping cities or landscapes. Drones offer high resolution and flexibility but come with a higher cost and require more expertise to operate.

Create a 3D model from your point cloud.

Import the point cloud data into CloudCompare.
In CloudCompare, you can preprocess and clean the point cloud if this is needed, as the data may contain noise or irrelevant points. If the data is too large, you can down sample the points or clip the area you want to focus on.
If your data consists of multiple point clouds from different scans or sources, you’ll need to align and register them into a single, unified point cloud. With CloudCompare, you can either automatically align or manually registering multiple point clouds.
Once you have a clear, aligned point cloud, you can generate a mesh (a 3D surface model) with the Poisson Surface Reconstruction tools.
Once you have a mesh, you can smooth or refine it to better represent the real-world surface.

You can now export it in various file formats, depending on your needs. Common formats include OBJ, STL, FBX, or PLY. You can even 3D print this!

title: 16  Roma al tempo di Benedetto XIV
text:
Figure 16.1: Map of Rome. From Roma al tempo di Benedetto XIV : la pianta di Roma di Giambattista Nolli del 1748 riprodotta da una copia Vaticana. Biblioteca Apostolica Vaticana:









Figure 16.2: Map of Rome. From Roma al tempo di Benedetto XIV : la pianta di Roma di Giambattista Nolli del 1748 riprodotta da una copia Vaticana. Biblioteca Apostolica Vaticana:



When most city maps were still bird’s eye perspective views, Giambattista Nolli produced a map of 18th century Rome which greatly reduced and systematised the information contained in the map (fig 12.1). Nolli limited himself to a 2d representation and only distinguished between public space (white) and private space (black). As a result, publicly accessible interior spaces like churches are visible in the map. Through reduction and abstraction, knowledge which otherwise remains hidden under the surface is instantly accessible. This is one of the basic goals of any analysis. Over the last decades, the Nolli map has mesmerised generations of urban designers, theorists and architects. Especially since the publication of “Learning from Las Vegas” (which also usedthe Nolli technique) dozens of “Nolli maps” have been produced.

title: 19  Studi per una Operante Storia Urbana di Venezia
text:
Figure 19.1: Forum von Pompeji. From Der Städtebau nach seinen künstlerischen Grundsätzen (4th ed. p. 3), by C. Sitte, 1909. Copyright 1983 by Friedr. Vieweg & Sohn Verlargsgesellschaft mbH, Braunschweig/Wiesbaden, No further use is allowed.



After the second world war, even a monumental city like Venice was in danger of large-scale modernisations that would have destroyed the old urban tissue. Saverio Muratori was one of the first architects to (unpopular at that time) raise his voice against this threat. He did this through a monumental documentation of the city in which he illustrated how Venice had grown through the centuries on the basis of very stable urban patterns. Muratori implied with his book that an understanding and appreciation of these patterns (and their vulnerability) was a basic requirement for architects and urban designers who wanted to design for the city. For Muratori, the basic elements of the city are buildings and configurations of buildings. This means that to understand these, one has to make a detailed survey of many individual buildings and areas in search for what they have in common. Like this, one can describe the basic building “types” which are used in Venice. An understanding of these types could help designers to avoid plans which are alien to the city. This book was the first of its kind and had an enormous influence in Italy, but also abroad. Muratori helped ground an Italian “school” in urban analysis. For more information about this, see the text by Anne Vernez Moudon elsewhere in this volume.
crumbs: 19  Studi per una Operante Storia Urbana di Venezia

title: 20  Learning from Las Vegas
text:
Figure 20.1



Before 1972, Las Vegas was regarded by many as an almost featureless and meaningless urban environment. This changed with the publication of this book. With the advent of the car- and media based culture in the nineteen sixties, a place like Las Vegas could suddenly acquire a completely different meaning; at least for architects and urban designers. This analysis suddenly made visible to the profession what had long been hidden under the surface: non-spaces and popular culture are powerful material for designers. A similar wish to find something unique in the everyday environment seems to drive many contemporary designers who try to represent phenomena like mobility, urban sprawl or the essence of the Randstad.

A traditional analysis of Las Vegas would have made little sense since the city has few traditional urban features. That is; fig. 19.1 shows that in fact Las Vegas is built up from the same elements as any city, only in a different mix. This is also made clear by their re-use of the Nolli map. A host of other new techniques is introduced, for instance in their visualisation of the importance of signs in Las Vegas and the use of photography.

title: 21  Bologna: politica e metodologia del restauro nei centri storici
text:
Figure 21.1



This is a good example of an analysis in the Italian tradition. Typically, these are based on meticulous surveys of the city. For Cervelatti, the most relevant source of knowledge about the city would probably be the building block, its characteristics and especially building typology. Conceptual abstractions like in many contemporary analyses (see for example Stadsportretten, Costa Iberica, Belvedere Bouwen) are obviously of a totally different nature. This analysis of Bologna begins with the city as a whole, but the information contained in the drawings is derived from a lower scale level. The drawings are not supposed to uncover a hidden truth about the city; they merely document its parts. In analyses like these, the factual information derived from a survey is as valuable and usable for design and policy as the conceptual force of many recent analyses.
crumbs: 21  Bologna: politica e metodologia del restauro nei centri storici

title: 22  Collage City
text:
Figure 22.1



Essential here is the so called “figure-ground” analysis (fig. 2-3); two carefully drawn illustrations where white represents public space and black represents built mass. The drawings themselves are not revolutionary (compare for instance to the Nolli-map), yet the opposition between the “traditional” city vs. the “modern” city (as already used in design by Le Corbusier) is made very clear and has made this study very influential.

In Rowe’s and Koetter’s view, neither pure adherence to modern urbanism, nor a fall back on the traditional city can be the answer to the contemporary urban design task. They seek the answer in what they call the collage city; a mix or “bricolage” where modern, freestanding typologies can exist side by side with a less specific and more traditional infill. Ancient Rome is presented as an illustration of the principle.

title: 23  Elements d’analyse urbaine
text:
Figure 23.1: Les illustrations des differents plans sont, sauf exception, empruntrees a des villes existantes. From Elements d’Analyse Urbaine, by P. Panerai, 1982.



Similar to this book, Elements d’analyse urbaine gives general principles and drawing examples for urban analysis. Their modification of the Nolli map and functional analysis below are good examples of simple but effective reduction drawings. Note also the drawings to the right which illustrate different kinds of urban growth. As a representative of the French school of urban analysis, this overview pays much attention to typological research, for example about housing typology in connection to city blocks. Interesting are the perspective drawings showing basic types of urban scenes. At first glance, the drawings and techniques might look outdated, but many of the examples you see in this book still use the same principles.

title: 24  Lecture d’une ville: Versailles
text: This is another example of a French School urban analysis. That means that apart from a number of introductory drawings on a larger scale, the emphasis is on building- and block typology. In addition to the palace, a large number of houses or “pavillons” were built in Versailles for the nobility and government officials. These were all based on the same typology, resulting in a very regular and formal urban environment (fig. 4). Although there were many variants of these houses and many have been extended or modified, the basic module is still recognisable. The book shows this basic module and some of its variants and characteristic details. Figs. 7-10 show how streets, squares and blocks were constructed from this. This urban layout has also survived, even though the tissue has become denser (fig.8). Especially fig. 11 is interesting because it clearly shows that a street is more than just the “white” in the map.

title: 25  Amsterdam als stedelijk bouwwerk
text:
Figure 25.1



Amsterdam als stedelijk bouwwerk was the first of its kind in the Netherlands. The study systematically analysed different parts of Amsterdam in a great number of drawings and an accompanying text. The emphasis is on the relationship between reality and an idealised or abstracted morphology. The writers look for patterns in the city structure in an attempt to find out what Amsterdam is.

Different areas are analysed with different drawing techniques. For the canal- zone, the emphasis is on the radial pattern formed by the canals and the streets. Its structure can be compared with ideal city plans such as those by Speckle and Stevin. Louwe and Van der Hoeven take up the canal zone and twist, cut and deform it to show its ordering principles. In fig. 3, they investigate whether we should read Amsterdam as an ideal military settlement like Speckle’s design. But the regularity in this plan is clearly absent in Amsterdam. Fig. 4 on the other hand shows the likeness between 17th century Amsterdam and the Stevin plan when the canal zone is “unrolled”.

Please note how in fig. 10, the actual state of the area around the Noorderkerk is constructed from an abstract pattern: as if the “designers” of the area had taken this pattern as a starting point. For the analysis of the Westelijke Tuinsteden, the drawings focus on the built mass, rather than on the public space. This limits the effect of the drawings somewhat since in the modern city, the space around buildings is often as relevant as the buildings themselves.

title: 26  Rotterdam Verstedelijkt Landschap
text:
Figure 26.1



The name of this book is a reference to “Amsterdam als Stedelijk Bouwwerk”, but there is a big difference in meaning: where Van der Hoeven and Louwe speak of Amsterdam as an “urban construction” (a man-made object, created ex nihilo, autonomous in space and time), Palmboom speaks of Rotterdam as an urbanised landscape: as something that evolved over time and remains forever linked to the landscape on which it is grounded. In the case of Rotterdam, this landscape is much more dynamic than in Amsterdam. Where Amsterdam developed along a small provincial river and an inland sea, Rotterdam is situated at the mouth of a big river and was always subjected to the forces of the open water (figs. 2-5). Naturally, the resulting complexity of the landscape has always shaped the layout of the city - from its street pattern to the layout of its green spaces. Together with later additions which do not respect the original landscape (like the highway system, fig. 6), this results in a city of separated “islands” (fig. 7). These islands all have their own internal logic and are sometimes poorly connected on a higher scale level (figs. 8). Also, the harbour and the reconstruction of the inner city after the second world war (figs. 9-10) increase the complexity. Palmboom pleads for an understanding of this complexity and the inevitable limits this sets for future developments: urban designers should not try to fight the fragmented nature of the city but cooperate with it and attempt to enhance existing qualities. Fig. 11 shows the main morphological layers which Palmboom distinguishes (landscape, city streets, and highways). Fig. 12 shows the structural diversity of the Rotterdam area in comparison to that of Amsterdam.

Also see: Habitat Expanding Architecture

title: 27  La Metropole Imaginaire: un Atlas de Paris
text:
Maps can be used to draw the city as it is, as it was and how it could have been. This book shows these stages for some areas in Paris. The presentation is simple but systematic and the result of much hard documentary work. Every chapter is preceded by an introductory text (not included here), two photographs to convey the atmosphere, some small drawings which show the development of the area, one or more maps showing part of the area in great detail and a beautiful exploded view. All the drawings are of high quality and follow the basic rules for analysis; the drawings have the same scale, the same orientation, the same kind of information, the same detail, the same frame etc. Unfortunately, the same rigour is not applied between the series, making it confusing for the reader to relate the one to the other. 
Although this way of analysing the city is comparable to say “Bologna”, the result is more poetic and the value for designers lies more in a comprehension of atmosphere and growth, than in concrete typological tools.
crumbs: 27  La Metropole Imaginaire: un Atlas de Paris

title: 28  Landschap en Verstedelijking tussen Den Haag en Rotterdam
text:
Figure 28.1: Open spaces. From Landschap en Verstedelijking tussen Den Haag en Rotterdam, by F. Palmboom, 1990.



This is a good example of how an analysis can be used as a basis for urban design. In this study, the landscape between Den Haag and Rotterdam is looked at from all sides; from its geomorphology to the traffic routes. Systematically presented theme maps are alternated with hand-drawn illustrations, summarising the argument. The reader is taken by the hand along all the steps that the designer took to understand the area. The last drawing shows the design proposal that was made possible with the analysis. Through such a systematic and yet intuitive process, the designer can indeed gain enough information for new design proposals. All decisions seem to derive from the analysis. On the one hand, this makes it easy for the reader or client to follow the designer’s reasoning, on the other hand, just because of its persuasive character, an analysis might often be used to justify a design which in fact has a wholly different agenda.
crumbs: 28  Landschap en Verstedelijking tussen Den Haag en Rotterdam

title: 29  Gli orizzonti della città diffusa
text: This analysis of different parts of Italy is based on a very close reading of regional maps. The time consuming preparation of the drawings is something this study has in common with earlier Italian analyses, although building typology is not considered here. The study draws attention to the nature of occupational patterns outside the cities and recent changes in this field. Please note how aerial photographs are used as a basis for some of the drawings. The quality of the drawings lies not only in the delicacy with which they were made but also in the careful selection of what is shown. Within the different series, there is strict adherence to basic drawing rules; unity of scale, orientation, framing, pen thickness etc. Mentioning this might seem banal, but clarity in the visual presentation of analyses is often very hard to obtain.
crumbs: 29  Gli orizzonti della città diffusa

title: 30  Point City - South City
text:
Figure 30.1: Forum von Pompeji. From S, M, L, XL, by R. Koolhaas (2nd ed.), 1998. Copyright 1995 by Rem Koolhaas and The Monacelli Press, Inc., All rights reserved under International and Pan-American Copyright Conventions.



O.M.A. and Rem Koolhaas have produced many influential urban designs accompanied by seductive analyses. Examples are their design for the Paris newtown Melun Senart, the proposal for the area around the Grande Arche, also in Paris, their design for Yokohama (included here) and many others. The present study was made for the Air Alexander manifestation which asked for design proposals for a Rotterdam suburb. The design team objected to this small scale focus and drew the brief into a totally different realm, touching the issue of urban density in the Netherlands in general. Basically, the study takes the then existing population of the Netherlands as a starting point and redistributes this according to several density models. This redistribution immediately puts claims of the Netherlands being “full” in a different perspective. While it is hard to call this a true morphological analysis, the study nevertheless uses familiar techniques and does mean to speak about spatial effects, albeit on an unfamiliar scale.

title: 31  Paris des Faubourgs: Formation, Transformation
text:
Figure 31.1



Paris des Faubourgs is a comprehensive study investigating the development of the areas which have grown around the old inner city of Paris: the Faubourgs. It includes maps, diagrams, photographs and texts which illustrate the social and urban relevance of these areas. This wide scope is characteristic for analyses of the French school. Our main interest is in the drawings. Figs. 2 - 4 show a morphological analysis of the area “cité des fleurs”; first as a basic section through a block, then as an assemblage of its various parts. The beauty of this analysis is that while one could look forever at the last drawing without learning much, the whole series clarifies the city-structure in a matter of seconds. The same goes for the transformation of the “plaine Monceau” in fig. 5. These drawings show how land ownership and circulation patterns have changed over time. Note that this is a very different series than in fig. 6 where the buildings in the area of Montmartre are included. All these analyses are excellent examples of how carefully drawn images can clarify complex urban patterns in a very short time.
crumbs: 31  Paris des Faubourgs: Formation, Transformation

title: 32  Het Land in de Stad: de stedebouw van de grote agglomeratie
text: One of the effects of urbanisation is the reduction of open land or the inclusion of pockets of open land in larger urban regions. Large urban regions each have their own typical city-land relationships (fig. 1). According the authors of “Het Land in de Stad” (the land in the city), planners and urbanists should use this fragmentation to their advantage to lessen the contrast and the distance between the city and the open. Green spaces have always attracted citizens and public institutions: here also, different cities each in their own way (fig.2). Surprisingly, the Dutch city of The Hague seems to have much more to offer in this respect than Amsterdam or Rotterdam. Fig.3 shows an interesting example of how to use morphological layers (see the chapter on analytical techniques elsewhere in this volume) and compare cities at the same time. Many times, morphological layers are drawn for only one case. Here, a small but relevant selection of layers enabled a clear comparison between several Dutch towns and how green spaces have been incorporated within the city proper.
crumbs: 32  Het Land in de Stad: de stedebouw van de grote agglomeratie

title: 33  Stadsanalyse: De Nieuwe Kaart van Den Haag / Stadsportretten
text:
Figure 33.1



Many times, an urban analysis is not meant to be read by a professional audience but by relatively inexperienced people. These might nonetheless have a great influence on the future of your plan: clients, politicians etc. In such cases, it is very important to make your message comprehensible at all costs. This means that you have to be very careful in the rhetoric of your story, that you select very carefully what you show and that you make your illustrations in such a way that the attention is not directed at the map, but at the message. The present analysis produced by the Urban Development section of the city of The Hague is a very clear example of this. Several short chapters in this study are illustrated with images that leave no room for doubt. The analysis starts with fig.1 which shows that The Hague has a very different relation to the national highway system than the other big cities in the west of Holland. This relation is as yet very weak, but the construction of a new tangent (fig. 3) will make new cross connections possible in the city (fig.4). The Hague has always had much better developed east-west connections than north-south. The reason for this is partly to be found in the geomorphology of the area (fig.6). But this illustration also shows more ways to conceptualise the city. A single image to summarise your argument can be a very important help in getting your ideas across (see for instance also projects Ijburg, Haveneiland en Rieteilanden. Here the authors have chosen for the image of a “bromvlieg” (blowfly - fig.8) that can be “healed” with a second wing in the form of the new road. 
The whole argument leads to the presentation of “The new map of The Hague”(fig.9). A document that would have been much more difficult to understand without the analysis.
crumbs: 33  Stadsanalyse: De Nieuwe Kaart van Den Haag / Stadsportretten

title: 34  Zee van Land
text:
Figure 34.1



This is a study of polders or “droogmakerijen” in the Netherlands. A large part of the country lies below sea level. In earlier times, this delta area was studded with lakes and swamps which were reclaimed from the seventeenth century onwards. The number and sizes of these polders are shown in fig 4. The internal structure of the polders was usually a grid; the size of which reflected contemporary requirements for agriculture and water management.

Fig. 5 shows a number of polders and the basic units which are part of their grid. The Beemster is used as an example to illustrate this. The grid of the Beemster has several layers. This is illustrated in figs. 6 and 7. The authors claim that even the internal structure of a single farm is connected directly to the higher grid levels. The overall layout of the polder is visualised in fig. 10. These simple, yet beautiful drawings immediately convey an image of what kind of place the Beemster is. Unfortunately, the measure with which the height was exaggerated is not indicated. One might think that the Beemster is actually that small. The drawings in this study are extremely clear and instructive. They have the power to give insight into a complex phenomenon in a short time. Exactly what an analysis should do.

title: 35  4, Edzo Bindels, Ruurd Gietema, Henk Hartzema, Arjan Klok
text:
Figure 35.1









Figure 35.2



“Grasstad” is a design for the Westelijke Tuinsteden in Amsterdam. The plan reinterprets the typical modernist features of this post war housing area (fig. 1). The beautiful series of drawings in fig. 3 is not an analysis of the present situation, but an analysis of the different structural layers of the new plan which follows overleaf. Compare this way of representing this area with the drawings shown in “Amsterdam als Stedelijk Bouwwerk”. Louwe and Van der Hoeven also tried to conceptualise the area but the concreteness of their analyses would have prevented a design proposal like this. Here, the existing typology is abandoned but the underlying principles are preserved. This abstract way of thinking is also far removed from the French and Italian analyses.

In “Weltevreden” the authors present an urban design on a very large scale. This creates the need for new ways of visualising the plan, but also new planning tools and design methods. Some of which can be seen here.

title: 36  Costa Iberica: upbeat to the leisure city
text: Many of MVRDV’s analyses are based on reinterpretations of density or related statistical data. This is an approach not unlike Rem Koolhaas’ in his analysis of Point City and South City. The present analysis looks at the impact of tourism on the landscape and economy of Spain and how one can take this as a departure for design. The main interest here is in the use of computer graphics which make a complicated and obscure starting point visible and understandable for everybody. The renderings almost take up a life of their own. The shape of the analysis could be confused with the actual landscape. Depending on your standpoint, this can result in nonsense or an inspiring allusion to possible spatial conditions. Costa Iberica in fact contains design proposals based on this material. These are not included here.

title: 37  Een nieuwe oude jas: de heruitvinding van stedelijke weefsels en woningtypes
text:
Links
Building blocks are often the basic material with which cities are built. Block sizes are inseparably connected to building typology. Width and height of a block limit the choice of buildings that will fit in and therefore influence the profitability of a plan. Block size and building typology also shape the city streets and interior spaces and consequently have a strong influence on the desired atmosphere of an area. Choices in block size and building typology are therefore basic material for urban designers. In this analysis a number of old and new blocks in Amsterdam are compared. It focuses on this relation between buildings and city form. The method can be compared to earlier French and Italian analyses such as Studi per una Operante Storia Urbana di Venezia, Bologna: politica e metodologia del restauro nei centri storici, Elements d’analyse urbaine, Lecture d’une ville: Versailles and “Les Bastides: d’Aquitaine, du Bas-Languedoc et du Béarn”, although there, the study would typically look into the buildings in more detail.

title: 38  Belvedere Bouwen: Vecht- en plassengebied
text:
Figure 38.1



This regional study attempts to characterise the river landscape and the building typologies of the Vechtstreek which consist for an important part of 17th and 18th century estates (fig. 4). The Vechtstreek is a beautiful area where official policy, until recently, was preservation-based, but where piecemeal growth has nevertheless resulted in a loss of character. This study is a good example of how an analysis can provide tools for both designers and policy- makers to allow growth which respects and enhances the traditional (see also Haarlemmermeer). It does so by establishing the basic units of the Vechtstreek, its “korrels” and to modify and compress these into a “sampled” unit which can be a basis for future design. 
The use of photography is an important aspect of the study. It is used for instance to illustrate the characteristics of a typical Vecht-village and to indicate how this differs from standard housing solutions (fig. 7). A second example is a visualisation of why a Michael Graves villa was considered to be of bad taste and how this could have been avoided (fig. 9).

Also see: Vecht Visie
crumbs: 38  Belvedere Bouwen: Vecht- en plassengebied

title: 39  IJburg, Haveneiland en Rieteilanden
text:
Figure 39.1



IJburg is a new extension to Amsterdam on new islands in the IJ-meer. The first drawings zoom into the area and show the position of IJburg relative to its surroundings. Each scale level shows information relevant to that level. Fig. 5 shows a simple comparative analysis where IJburg is compared to other well known parts of Amsterdam. The same goes for fig. 8 where the morphology of IJburg is compared. The grid-structure of the islands is put into a clear perspective when it is shown next to other grid areas in Amsterdam; the reader and designer can get a feel for the area. Fig. 6 and 7 show the principles to which the block designs should adhere in an abstract way. One should not underestimate the power of these little drawings. During the course of the design process, (which can take up to four or five years) these drawings can always be used by the different parties to remind each other of the basic principles. Fig. 9 shows the way the grid- structure is developed on the new land. Compare this for example to the drawings in “Amsterdam als Stedelijk Bouwwerk”.

title: 40  Mobility: a room with a view
text:
The highway has changed from a means to get from one place to the other into an end in itself. Many people spend a considerable part of their life on the road. The highway and increased mobility should not be considered a necessary evil, but as an urban phenomenon in its own right; obviously not only in Holland, but all over the world - or so the authors claim.

When the highway is considered a “place”, then ways have to be found to represent its characteristics, much like Venturi et al had to do when they proclaimed the Las Vegas strip the typical representative of contemporary life. In their analysis of the randstad, the authors have tried to illustrate the principle of mobility in a map where towns are renamed according to the role in one person’s life. Next to that on the same scale is a map of the ring road connecting the cities within the randstad. Further illustrations are abstractions of that map. Ideally, when the highway is considered an urban design task, drivers might be able to enjoy it in the way foreseen in fig. 9.
crumbs: 40  Mobility: a room with a view

title: 41  Haarlemmermeer
text:
A final example of an analysis which separates a map in layers to uncover basic structures. The Haarlemmermeer is the biggest polder in the Netherlands. Due to its central location in the Randstad and the presence of our national airport Schiphol, there is a tremendous economic pressure on this polder. As a result, also some main infrastructural works cross the area: the Amsterdam-Rotterdam highway and several railway lines, including the new high speed connection to Paris. The economic pressure has never been counterbalanced by an appreciation of the Haarlemmermeer as an important part of our cultural heritage. It served simply as a very convenient trash-can for large scale development in the vicinity of Amsterdam. Over the last few years, Designers and government have opened their eyes to cultural historic values and have tried to find ways to allow for further economic development without destroying the landscape (see also Belvedere Bouwen: Vecht- en plassengebied). In this analysis, Steenbergen and Reh separate the original landscape from later additions to isolate what is valuable and to find room for responsible growth.

Fig. 2 shows the “polder grammar”: a large quadrant of grid units in the centre, a number of added units to the sides and an edge that does not fit in the grid. Fig.3 shows the urban “additions”: towns, industrial areas and the airport. Fig.4 shows a superposition of these, resulting in fig.5, where we see that there is only one grid unit left which is untouched by later additions. If one has isolated the basic elements of the polder (old and new), one can draw several design options that can enhance some and spare others. Some variants for further urbanisation can be seen in figs. 8-10. This analysis uses the same techniques as Zee van Land by the same authors.

title: 45  The View From The Road
text:
Kevin Lynch’ study addresses the faster movement of the automobile. The cover photograph of the book summarises the complex visual experience of the car driver: different speeds, different horizons, different perspectives at the same time. In this study, Lynch attempts to bring this complex experience into the realm of spatial design. If we document the view from the road, we may make better designs for the road. 
He does this in two ways: first by documenting scenes or events along the way and translating them into a symbolic legend and linear drawings. Second, by drawing maps in which this linear experience is brought back to the actual shape of the city, leading to fascinating and beautiful drawings, suggestive of much more than summarised by the rather straightforward word “road”.

title: 46  Ephemeral Urbanisms: Kumbh Mela, India
text:
Figure 46.1: Kumbh Mela Festival, by Dinesh Mehta. From Ephemeral Urbansim: Does permanence matter? (2nd ed. p. 320), by R. Merhotra et al., 2022. Copyright 2022 by ListLab, No further use is allowed.



The increased acceleration of human movement challenges permanence as a default condition of the city. It becomes ever more relevant, therefore, to study examples of temporary settlements, or ephemeral urbanisms: over 700 million of the global population are currently living in spaces of flux.

The Kumbh Mela, a Hindu celebration that takes place every 12 years, is the worlds’ largest religious gathering. It takes places over 55 days in India, on the floodplain between two sacred rivers: the Ganges and the Yamuna. The physical geography of the floodplain is highly dynamic and heavily affected by the movement of the monsoon, and so it is necessary for this temporary megacity to have fluid edges.

The grid defines the infrastructure network, but the morphology of the floodplain is only evident once the monsoon has passed, so the grid is adapted and shifts from year to year. City is a development of uncertainties. Grid provides each visiting community with agency over their own spatial organisation. Water, electricity, sewage, roads, bridge all organised by the grid, that connects some of the more permanent infrastructure with the temporary one that comes back every 12 years.

title: 47  Urban Taxonomy
text:
Links
The Urban Taxonomy is an example of typology construction that uses hierarchical morphotope classification. It builds upon Conzen’s notion of a morphotope: the smallest unit of morphologically homogenous land and uses these to identify patterns and cluster morphologically similar areas together. This method works by ‘clustering’ similar points in a given dataset, thereby allowing you to identify different groups, or typologies. This approach allows you to process and analyse large datasets with many variables that would be impossible to do manually. In the Urban Taxonomy, patterns of urban form are classified into the following typologies of urban fabric: Coherent Interconnected Fabric, Coherent Dense Adjacent Fabric, Coherent Dense Disjoint Fabric, Incoherent Large-Scale Homogenous Fabric, Incoherent, Large-Scale Heterogenous Fabric, Incoherent Small-Scale Linear Fabric, Incoherent Small-Scale Sparse Fabric, and Incoherent Small-Scale Compact Fabric. As can be seen in Figure 1, the clear graphic style of an analysis like this allows you to easily compare between different cities at the same scale.
